name: kept-vs-code-mode
title: A kept script is data, not a program
part: What it costs, and how it was built
html:
A kept script is data, not a program

# release.heart.yaml (excerpt), kept by artie generate
heart: 1
kind: kept
steps:
  - act: scm:pulls-get
    fields: {owner: ${owner}, repo: ${repo},
             pull_number: ${pull}}
    then: [keep-as: pr]
  - enter: ${watcher}
    steps:
      - ask: watcher:watch
        fields: {resource: ${pr.@self},
                 offers: scm:merge}
  - once-answered: {reply: watch, steps: […
      - act: scm:merge
        fields: {method: squash}
# release.pins.yaml: what each form was, by hash
  scm:merge: {method: PUT,
    integrity: sha256-sGUdrPfH…}

release.heart.yaml release.pins.yaml

Kept YAML (ARTIE)

  • Data. No loops, imports or eval to review.
  • Every act names a relation the server must still offer.
  • Pinned by hash: a changed form stops the replay.
  • Runs with no model, in any HEART client.

Code Mode

  • The model writes TypeScript or Python against tool APIs.
  • What you keep is a program: code review, sandbox, dependencies.
  • It can call anything its bindings expose, in any order.
  • A real step up from tool lists in context.
say: Code Mode (Cloudflare, September 2025; Anthropic's code execution with MCP, November 2025) has the model write TypeScript against tool APIs and runs it in a sandbox. That's a real improvement on stuffing tool lists into context. But what you keep is a program: it needs code review, a sandbox, dependency hygiene, and it can call anything its bindings expose. ARTIE keeps YAML: no loops you didn't capture, no imports, no eval. Every act names a relation, and before it's sent ARTIE checks the form is still offered and still matches its pin. A review is reading data.
